blocks.s: Denis confesses the darkness of his own understanding before these words, yet explains as best he can. The foundation of the contemplative's essence or being can be understood in two ways. First, God himself is understood by it — the fontal stabilization and causal foundation of all beings, which is unshakeable and incomprehensible: and the contemplative must attend to this lest he presumptuously intrude upon the divine mysteries, and so become a searcher of majesty and be overwhelmed by glory (cf. Prov. 25:27). He must, therefore, possess this foundation — which is above all things yet not exalted, below all things yet not oppressed, grounding, upholding, and conserving all — by gracious and affectionate contemplation as an utterly unsearchable being, knowing that he can in no way comprehend it.

Second, the foundation of the contemplative's essence can be understood as his own fundamental being — his own proper nature — which (as regards all that pertains to himself) cannot be fathomed by us, especially as regards his supernatural being, namely of sanctifying grace, and most of all as regards that which belongs to him through the singular grace of sublime contemplation. In this grace, the inmost and most secret being of the mind, emptied and stripped of all creaturely things, is so advanced and fixed in God by a most gracious union, that it is found to fail even in its own self-examination and self-distinction.
